newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: N.Ireland a top Labour government priority -Blair.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland a top Labour government priority -Blair.

text.p: Opposition Labour party leader Tony Blair told the Irish government on Thursday that there would be no change to Britain's Northern Ireland policy, the cause of current strains between London and Dublin, if he wins general elections due by next May.

Blair reassured Irish Prime Minister John Bruton that a Labour government would continue to make the Northern Ireland conflict a top priority but signalled no change towards the demands of the ruling Conservative party for a credible, verifiable IRA guerrilla truce.

He echoed British Prime Minister John Major's insistence that any Irish Republican Army ceasefire would have to be permanent before its Sinn Fein political wing could be admitted to Northern Ireland peace talks under way in Belfast.
Britain must hold a general election in the next five months and Blair's Labour Party has a huge lead over Major's Conservatives in opinion polls.
Blair was in Dublin to attend a meeting of European Union socialist leaders ahead of an summit which starts on Friday.

He said the IRA had to satisfy the government that a new truce would be "sincere, that it is going to last" and said a Labour government would decide itself whether a ceasefire was a genuine end to the 27-year IRA war against British rule or a tactical ploy.

Sinn Fein, which shares the IRA's goal of an end to British rule of Northern Ireland and reunification with the Irish republic, is excluded from the talks because of the IRA's failure to call a lasting truce.

It ended a 17-month ceasefire in February with a bombing campaign in Britain and Northern Ireland and Major told Bruton on Monday that any new IRA truce would have to mean a renunciation of violence altogether before Sinn Fein could join the negotiations.

This disappointed Bruton's government, which wants Sinn Fein to be admitted to the talks automatically and immediately rather than waiting for the British government to decide if the truce is genuine or not.
The Irish government is concerned that a Labour administration might downgrade Northern Ireland to tackle issues such as education and the health service.
But Blair promised Bruton that a Labour government would continue to make the quest for a lasting settlement between pro-British Unionists and Irish nationalists a top agenda item.

"My commitment to the peace process is every bit as great as that of the current government," Blair told reporters after talks with Bruton, Foreign Minister Dick Spring and opposition leader Bertie Ahern.
Bruton expressed dismay at the discovery of a suspected IRA mortar in an alleyway.

"It is important that the Republican movement make up its mind whether it is interested in the peace process or not, " he said. "I believe the Irish people want this to stop. There is absolutely no mandate from the Irish people for this violence."
